How to Read Your Pay Stub, Line by Line (With a Worked Sample)

Direct AnswerLearn to read your pay stub line by line: gross pay, FICA, federal and state withholding, pre-tax vs post-tax deductions, and YTD — with a worked sample stub.

Gross pay estimates
By Saahil•Published October 29, 2026•12 min read•Payroll & Compensation
A closer look

In this guide

The Short Answer: Read Top to BottomA Complete Sample Pay StubTop of the Stub: Who, When, and How OftenEarnings: What You Were Paid ForDeductions, in the Order They Come OutCodes and Abbreviations, DecodedThe YTD Column: Your Built-in AuditSpot an Error in 5 MinutesIf Something Looks WrongHow to Use the CalculatorLimitationsFrequently Asked QuestionsKey Takeaways & Action Plan

Use your actual work schedule for a more useful estimate.

Quick Answer

Read a pay stub top to bottom: header (who and which pay period), earnings (gross pay), deductions in order (pre-tax benefits, FICA, income-tax withholding, post-tax items), then net pay — with a year-to-date column beside every line for a running check.

The Short Answer: Read Top to Bottom

Every pay stub, whatever the payroll provider, tells the same story in the same order. At the top: who you are, who employs you, and which days this check covers. In the middle: what you earned — regular hours, overtime, and anything extra — added up into gross pay. Below that: everything taken out, line by line, in a specific order that matters more than most people realise. At the bottom: net pay, the amount that actually reaches your bank account. And beside almost every line, a second column labelled YTD — year-to-date — that quietly audits the whole year.

The single most useful habit is this: never start at net pay. Start at gross pay, follow each deduction down, and confirm the arithmetic yourself — gross minus deductions equals net. If it does not, something is wrong, and this guide shows you how to find it in about five minutes. The sample stub below is fictional, but every number in it ties out exactly, so you can practise the checks on real arithmetic before opening your own stub.

A Complete Sample Pay Stub

Meet our example worker: hourly, $28 an hour, paid biweekly. This check covers the pay period October 12–25, 2026, paid October 30, 2026 — the 20th paycheck of the year. She worked 80 regular hours and 4 overtime hours. Here is her whole stub, current period and year-to-date side by side:

LineCurrent periodYear-to-date
Regular pay (80 hrs × $28.00)$2,240.00$44,800.00
Overtime pay (4 hrs × $42.00)$168.00$3,360.00
Gross pay$2,408.00$48,160.00
Health premium (pre-tax)− $120.00− $2,400.00
401(k), 5% of gross (pre-tax)− $120.40− $2,408.00
Social Security, 6.2%− $141.86− $2,837.20
Medicare, 1.45%− $33.18− $663.60
Federal withholding− $176.27− $3,525.40
State withholding (illustrative 4%)− $86.70− $1,734.00
Supplemental life (post-tax)− $8.50− $170.00
Total deductions− $686.91− $13,738.20
Net pay$1,721.09$34,421.80

Figure 1: A complete biweekly pay stub. Every line ties out: $2,408.00 gross minus $686.91 deductions equals $1,721.09 net, and every YTD figure is exactly 20 times the current figure because this is the 20th identical check of the year.

Two facts to carry from this table. First, the worker keeps about 71.5 cents of every gross dollar on this check ($1,721.09 ÷ $2,408.00). Second, the order of the deduction lines is not cosmetic: the health premium comes out before the tax lines because it changes the wages the taxes are calculated on, while the 401(k) changes only some of them. The rest of this guide walks each section in that order.

Top of the Stub: Who, When, and How Often

The header looks boring, and that is exactly why errors hide there. Check four things before you read a single dollar figure:

  • Your name and employee ID: a stub for the wrong person is rarer than it sounds, but a wrong ID can send deductions to the wrong record.
  • Pay period vs pay date: the pay period is the days you worked (here October 12–25); the pay date is when the money lands (October 30). If a check feels short, the pay period is the first suspect — a holiday week or a late timesheet can shift hours into the next period.
  • Pay frequency: weekly, biweekly, semimonthly, or monthly. Frequency changes how deductions are split: the same annual health premium is a smaller slice of a biweekly check than of a monthly one, and biweekly pay produces two three-paycheck months a year. Our biweekly vs semimonthly guide and three-paycheck-months guide explain both effects.
  • Direct deposit account: many stubs print the last four digits of the account paid. If those digits are not yours, stop and call payroll before anything else.

Salaried workers get a simpler header section: no hours column, just the salary amount for the period. The rest of the stub — deductions, YTD, net — works exactly the same way.

Earnings: What You Were Paid For

Earnings lines answer one question: what did you do to earn this check? For hourly workers, each line shows a rate, hours, and amount, and the amounts must add up to gross pay. On our sample:

StepMathResult
Step 1 — Regular pay80 hours × $28.00$2,240.00
Step 2 — Overtime rate$28.00 × 1.5$42.00 per hour
Step 3 — Overtime pay4 hours × $42.00$168.00
Gross pay$2,240.00 + $168.00$2,408.00

Lines beyond regular and overtime appear often enough to recognise: shift differential (extra pay for nights or weekends), bonus or commission (often withheld at the flat 22% federal supplemental rate, which looks high but settles at tax time), PTO, holiday, and sick pay (paid time off, still gross pay), and retro pay (a correction for an earlier period — if a mystery amount appears, retro pay is the usual explanation). Our overtime tax guide clears up why an overtime-heavy check can look over-taxed when it is not.

Honesty note: earnings lines show what payroll recorded, not necessarily what you worked. Compare the hours against your own timecard or schedule every period — a missing overtime hour is the most common small error, and it is cheapest to fix in the same pay period.

Deductions, in the Order They Come Out

This is the section most guides rush past, and it is where the real money hides. Deductions come out in an order, and the order decides what the taxes are calculated on. Three wage bases matter:

Wage baseHow it is built (sample stub)Amount
Gross payRegular + overtime$2,408.00
FICA wagesGross − Section 125 health premium only$2,288.00
Income-tax wagesGross − health premium − 401(k)$2,167.60

Now each deduction line, in stub order:

  • Pre-tax benefits first. The $120.00 health premium is a Section 125 cafeteria-plan deduction, so it lowers both FICA wages and income-tax wages. The $120.40 401(k) contribution (5% of gross) lowers income-tax wages only — FICA is still calculated on pay before the 401(k). That asymmetry is the single most misunderstood line on a stub, and our 401(k) impact calculator shows exactly how it changes take-home pay.
  • FICA next. Social Security 6.2% of FICA wages ($2,288.00 × 6.2% = $141.86) up to the 2026 wage base of $184,500, and Medicare 1.45% of all FICA wages ($2,288.00 × 1.45% = $33.18). Together: $175.04, or 7.65% of FICA wages. Our FICA guide covers the wage base, the extra 0.9% Medicare tax above $200,000, and the employer match.
  • Income-tax withholding next. Federal withholding ($176.27 here) is set by your Form W-4 and the IRS withholding tables, which annualise your pay — it is not your tax bracket applied to one check, so you cannot reproduce it exactly from the stub alone. State withholding ($86.70, shown at an illustrative 4%) depends on your state; some states levy no income tax at all. Our paycheck tax guide walks the full withholding calculation.
  • Post-tax items last. The $8.50 supplemental life premium comes out after all taxes, so it reduces net pay dollar for dollar without reducing any tax. Garnishments and Roth 401(k) contributions also sit here.

Employer-paid lines sometimes appear in a separate column — the employer’s FICA match, its share of your health premium, its 401(k) match. Those are not deductions from your pay; they are part of your total compensation, and they should never be subtracted from your gross.

Codes and Abbreviations, Decoded

Payroll providers love abbreviations, and the same tax can wear several names. The ones you will meet most:

CodeMeaningWhat to know
FICA / SS / OASDISocial Security tax6.2% up to the $184,500 wage base (2026); OASDI is the formal name for the same tax
MED / HIMedicare tax1.45% of all wages; HI stands for Hospital Insurance, Medicare’s formal name
FIT / FEDFederal income-tax withholdingSet by your W-4; not your final tax bill
SIT / STState income-tax withholdingAbsent in states with no income tax
401(k) / 403(b)Retirement contributionPre-tax for income tax; does not reduce FICA
125 / CAF / MED PRESection 125 cafeteria planHealth premiums that reduce both FICA and income-tax wages
HSA / FSAHealth savings / flexible spendingPre-tax; HSA money is yours to keep, FSA money usually is not
GTLGroup-term life imputed incomeNot a deduction — taxable value of employer life cover above $50,000, added to wages
GARNGarnishmentCourt- or agency-ordered withholding; comes out post-tax

Codes vary by provider, so a code missing from this table is not automatically an error — ask payroll what it stands for and whether it is an employee deduction or an employer contribution before assuming either.

The YTD Column: Your Built-in Audit

YTD — year-to-date — is the running total of each line since January 1, and it does three jobs no other column can. First, it catches slow errors: a wrong rate on one check is easy to miss, but a YTD line drifting from your own records over months is not. Second, it previews your W-2: YTD gross, federal withholding, and Social Security wages should land close to the matching W-2 boxes at year end (small differences come from pre-tax items the W-2 treats differently). Third, it exposes resets: YTD figures should never drop mid-year except when a new calendar year starts or you change employers.

The quick YTD check on our sample: divide any YTD figure by the number of paychecks so far. YTD gross $48,160.00 ÷ 20 checks = $2,408.00, exactly the current gross. YTD net $34,421.80 ÷ 20 = $1,721.09, exactly the current net. If your own stub’s YTD divided by check count does not roughly equal the current figure, something changed mid-year — a raise, a benefits election, a missed check — and it is worth knowing which.

One more YTD habit: compare this stub’s YTD with the previous stub’s YTD. The difference should equal this check’s current figures, line by line. If it does not, a correction landed somewhere, and payroll can point to it.

Spot an Error in 5 Minutes

Run these five checks on any stub, in order. All five use the sample stub’s numbers so you can see each check pass:

CheckMathResult
1 — Earnings add up$2,240.00 + $168.00$2,408.00 gross ✓
2 — Overtime rate is 1.5×$28.00 × 1.5$42.00 ✓
3 — FICA is 7.65% of FICA wages$141.86 + $33.18 vs $2,288.00 × 7.65%$175.04 vs $175.03 — a penny of rounding ✓
4 — Net ties out$2,408.00 − $686.91$1,721.09 ✓
5 — YTD ÷ checks matches$48,160.00 ÷ 20$2,408.00 ✓

Check 3 deserves its footnote: Social Security and Medicare are each rounded to the cent before they are added, so the pair can sit a penny away from a single 7.65% calculation. A penny is rounding. A FICA total that is a whole percent off — say 7.65% of gross instead of FICA wages, or a Social Security line that keeps charging past the wage base — is a real error. The same tolerance applies to net pay: a penny is rounding, anything more is a question.

Also compare net pay with the deposit that actually arrived. Split deposits, a separate reimbursement, or bank timing can explain a gap — but the stub’s net and the deposit should match once those are accounted for.

If Something Looks Wrong

Most stub errors are small and fixable, but they compound if ignored — a wrong rate repeats every period, and a wrong W-4 repeats every check until you file a new one. Work this ladder:

  1. Compare against your own records first. Timecard hours, offer-letter rate, benefits elections you actually signed. Half of all "errors" turn out to be a forgotten election or a pay period that does not cover the days you assumed.
  2. Take the exact line to payroll, in writing. "My overtime line shows 3 hours; my timecard shows 4" gets fixed faster than "my check looks short." Keep a copy of the stub and your records.
  3. Fix the cause, not just the check. A rate error needs a payroll correction; a withholding surprise needs a new Form W-4 (file it any time, not just at hiring); a benefits error needs an election change. Ask payroll whether the fix applies retroactively or only from the next check.
  4. Keep your stubs. They are your evidence if a W-2 is wrong, if a premium was over-collected, or if an employer record disappears. A year of stubs plus the final W-2 is the complete paper trail.

One thing a stub cannot tell you: whether your withholding will match your final tax bill. Withholding is an estimate collected across the year; the return settles the difference. If a stub’s federal line looks nothing like your expectation, our paycheck tax guide shows how the annualised withholding math works, and the IRS Tax Withholding Estimator can confirm whether a new W-4 is warranted.

How to Use the Calculator

Test your own stub against the same arithmetic in four steps:

  1. Step 1 — Enter your pay: put your hourly rate, hours, and pay frequency into the paycheck calculator.
  2. Step 2 — Add your deductions: enter your pre-tax benefits and retirement contribution the way they appear on your stub.
  3. Step 3 — Compare the lines: match the calculator’s gross, FICA, and net against your stub’s lines — the FICA and gross lines should agree closely; the federal line will differ because withholding follows your W-4.
  4. Step 4 — Try a change: raise the 401(k) percent or add overtime hours and watch which lines move — FICA moves with health premiums but not with 401(k), exactly as this guide explains.

Limitations

Keep these limits in mind before using any figure above as a budget:

  1. One fictional sample: the sample stub is a teaching example with identical checks all year. Real stubs vary — raises, bonuses, and benefits changes break the neat YTD pattern, and that is normal.
  2. Withholding is illustrative: the federal and state lines follow a single filer’s W-4 and an illustrative 4% state rate. Your withholding depends on your W-4, your state, and your total income, and it is an estimate, not your final tax bill.
  3. State and local rules vary: some states have no income tax, some tax at flat rates, and some cities add their own withholding. This guide uses federal rules plus one illustrative state line.
  4. Provider formats differ: line names, codes, and column layouts vary by payroll provider. The order and the arithmetic are universal; the labels are not.
  5. Not tax or legal advice: this guide explains how to read a stub. For a dispute about pay, withholding, or a garnishment, payroll — and, if needed, a tax professional — is the right next step.

Frequently Asked Questions

The questions readers ask most about reading a pay stub:

What is the difference between gross pay and net pay on a pay stub?

Gross pay is everything you earned in the pay period before anything is taken out; net pay is what is left after all taxes and deductions and is the amount that reaches your bank account. On the sample stub in this guide, gross pay of $2,408.00 becomes net pay of $1,721.09 after $686.91 of deductions — about 71.5% of gross.

Why is my federal withholding different from my coworker’s on the same pay?

Federal withholding follows the Form W-4 you filed, not just your pay: filing status, dependents and credits in Step 3, extra withholding in Step 4(c), and any second job all change the amount. Two people with identical gross pay can legitimately see different federal lines, and neither is necessarily wrong.

What does FICA mean on my pay stub?

FICA is the umbrella term for the two federal payroll taxes: Social Security (6.2% of wages up to the $184,500 wage base in 2026) and Medicare (1.45% of all wages, plus an extra 0.9% once yearly wages pass $200,000). Together they are 7.65% of your FICA wages, and your employer matches that amount separately.

Do 401(k) contributions lower Social Security and Medicare taxes?

No. A traditional 401(k) contribution lowers your federal and (in most states) state income-tax wages, but not your FICA wages — Social Security and Medicare are still calculated on pay before the 401(k) comes out. Health premiums under a Section 125 cafeteria plan are different: they lower both income-tax wages and FICA wages.

What is YTD on a pay stub, and why should I check it?

YTD (year-to-date) is the running total of each line since January 1. It is your built-in audit: divide any YTD figure by the number of paychecks so far and you should get roughly the current-period figure, and the YTD gross and tax totals should closely match your W-2 at year end. A YTD line that jumps or resets mid-year is worth a question to payroll.

My net pay is lower than I expected. What should I check first?

Check in this order: pay period dates (did this check cover the days you think?), hours and rate on the earnings lines, the pre-tax vs post-tax split of your deductions, and whether a one-off line appeared (a bonus, a correction, or a benefits catch-up). If the arithmetic still does not tie out — gross minus deductions does not equal net — take the stub to payroll with the exact line circled.

Key Takeaways & Action Plan

  • Read top to bottom: header, earnings, deductions in order, net pay — and never start at net pay.
  • Order matters: health premiums lower FICA and income-tax wages; 401(k) lowers income-tax wages only.
  • The sample ties out exactly: $2,408.00 gross − $686.91 deductions = $1,721.09 net, about 71.5% of gross.
  • FICA is 7.65% of FICA wages (6.2% Social Security + 1.45% Medicare), not of gross pay — a penny of rounding is fine, a percent off is an error.
  • YTD is your audit: divide any YTD line by checks so far, and compare each YTD with the previous stub’s YTD.
  • Errors compound: flag a wrong line to payroll in writing, in the same pay period, and keep your stubs for the W-2 check.

Sources & Method

The sample stub is fictional and constructed so every line ties out exactly: 80 regular hours at $28.00 plus 4 overtime hours at $42.00 (time-and-a-half) gives $2,408.00 gross; the Section 125 health premium of $120.00 reduces both FICA wages ($2,288.00) and income-tax wages ($2,167.60 after the 5% 401(k) contribution of $120.40); Social Security 6.2% and Medicare 1.45% use 2026 federal rates and the $184,500 Social Security wage base, per IRS rules and our FICA guide; federal withholding of $176.27 follows the annualised single-filer method (2026 standard deduction $16,100, brackets 10% to $12,400, 12% to $50,400, per IRS Revenue Procedure 2025-32); the state line is illustrative at 4% of income-tax wages. State and local rules vary and are not included except where noted. This article is general information, not tax advice.

3 Things to Remember

  1. Read top to bottom — header, earnings, deductions in order, net pay — and check the YTD column beside every line.
  2. Pre-tax benefits change the wages taxes are calculated on: health premiums lower both FICA and income-tax wages, 401(k) only income-tax wages.
  3. Five minutes of checks — earnings add up, overtime is 1.5×, FICA is 7.65% of FICA wages, net ties out, YTD divides cleanly — catches most stub errors.

Methodology & Data Verification

  • Basis: Pay figures are gross unless a section states take-home; tax figures use 2026 federal rules where shown.
  • Method: Full formulas, baselines, and rounding rules are on our calculation methodology page.
  • Coverage: U.S. federal rules; state and local rules vary and are not included.
  • Review: Last updated October 29, 2026.
  • Disclaimer: Estimates for planning only — not tax or legal advice.
